Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Develop an understanding of the clinical presentation and radiographic findings of
inflammatory spinal arthritides to aid in early diagnosis and management.
Learn how rheumatoid arthritis may contribute to unique patterns of cervical spine instability,
and review the indications for surgical management.
Gain an understanding of the medical comorbidities associated with rheumatoid arthritis and
insight into what pharmacologic agents should be continued or withheld before elective
surgery.
Learn how the seronegative spondyloarthropathies (such as ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic
arthritis, reactive arthritis, and enteropathic spondyloarthropathy) are distinct from
rheumatoid arthritis.
Perform a diagnostic workup and formulate a plan for patients with ankylosing spondylitis who
experience traumatic injury to the spinal column.

Rheumatoid Arthritis
Background and Epidemiology
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic systemic inflammatory disease that is characterized by
synovial inflammation and hyperplasia, autoantibody production, cartilage and bone
destruction, and systemic cardiovascular and pulmonary disease.
Rheumatoid factor is an immunoglobulin that is directed against the antigens of targeted
synovial cells. This antigen-antibody interaction leads to the release of proteolytic enzymes
that destroy the joint.
An increased risk for rheumatoid arthritis is observed in patients in whom environmental
factors, such as smoking and periodontitis, exist in the presence of genetic factors, such as
individuals with the HLA-DR1 or HLA-DR4 serotypes.
It is the most common inflammatory arthritis, with an estimated incidence of 20 to 50 cases
per 100,000 persons in North America1 (Resource 1).
1% to 2% of the population is affected.
Symptoms typically begin in patients aged between 20 and 45 years.
70% of patients affected by rheumatoid arthritis are female.
The course of the disease is unpredictable and may be progressive or characterized by
intermittent flares and remissions.
It is a chronic disease without a cure.
Extra-articular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis include cardiovascular disease,
interstitial lung disease, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

Background and Epidemiology
Primarily, rheumatoid arthritis affects the synovial membrane of the smaller joints of the
appendicular skeleton in a symmetric fashion. Progressive joint swelling, pain, and
stiffness develop secondary to synovitis. Spinal involvement is most prevalent in the
cervical spine; however, pain attributable to inflammation and joint degeneration may
develop throughout the spinal column. Erosive synovitis observed in patients with
rheumatoid arthritis is believed to be the result of an immune response to an antigen
expressed by the synovial cells. An increased number of CD4 lymphocytes that activate B
lymphocytes to produce immunoglobulin frequently is found in the synovium in patients

with rheumatoid arthritis. The activation of macrophages results in the production of
tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, interleukins, and intracellular signaling, which, in turn,
attract additional lymphocytes and neutrophils.1 Modern therapies target pro-
inflammatory elements of this cascade.
Rheumatoid Cervical Spondylitis
Spinal disease eventually occurs in approximately 60% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
The cervical spine is composed of 22 separate synovial joints, which places this region of the
body at higher risk for clinical manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis.
There are three main patterns of instability: atlantoaxial subluxation, basilar invagination, and
subaxial subluxation.

Rheumatoid Cervical Spondylitis
Patients with more severe disease and longer duration of disease are at higher risk for
cervical spine involvement. The atlantoaxial joint connects the atlas (C1) with the axis
(C2) and is primarily responsible for rotation of the cervical spine. The zygapophysial and
uncovertebral joints also are synovial joints. Erosion of the odontoid process may occur
anteriorly at its synovial joint with the arch of C1 or posteriorly at its synovial joint with
the transverse ligament. Erosion also may occur at the tip of the odontoid in relation to
the apical ligament insertion. Depending on the pattern of erosion, and laxity of
supporting ligaments, various radiographic instability patterns may result, including AP,
rotatory, or lateral subluxation2 (Resource 2).
Atlantoaxial Subluxation
Atlantoaxial subluxation is the most common form of instability, present in more than 50% of
patients with RA.
It is most commonly due to anterior subluxation of C1 on C2 as a result of pannus formation
between the dens and the ring of C1 that leads to destruction of the dens and the transverse
ligament.

The anterior subluxation of C1 on C2 results in reduced space available for the cord.
Pannus formation may further contribute to spinal cord compression (Figure 1).
Instability is defined as greater than 3.5 mm of translational motion between flexion and
extension views.
Greater than 10 mm of translational motion is an indication for surgical management given the
increased risk of neurologic injury.
Figure 1 Images of the cervical spine of a 65-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and
progressive cervical myelopathy. A, Lateral radiograph demonstrates atlantoaxial subluxation.
The anterior atlanto-dens interval is 4 mm and the posterior atlanto-dens interval is 14 mm.
Sagittal (B) and axial (C) T2-weighted MRIs show substantial additional reduction in space
available for the cord to 7 mm because of a large soft-tissue pannus posterior to the odontoid
process. (Reproduced with permission from Kim DH, Hilibrand AS: Rheumatoid arthritis in the
cervical spine. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2005;13[7]:463-474.)

Atlantoaxial Subluxation
Atlantoaxial subluxation may occur without substantial degrees of peripheral disease in
patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Risk factors for progression of atlantoaxial
subluxation include male sex, rheumatoid factor seropositivity, higher initial C-reactive
protein level, presence of subcutaneous nodules, and advanced peripheral joint
disease.2-4 Posterior subluxation occurs if C1 moves posterior to C2 and is the result of
erosion or fracture of the odontoid. Lateral subluxation occurs with erosion of the lateral
mass and the odontoid.

Basilar Invagination
Basilar invagination is thought to occur subsequent to atlantoaxial subluxation.5
Superior migration of the odontoid occurs from bony erosion between the atlanto-occipital
and atlantoaxial joints or from bilateral erosion of the lateral masses.

Basilar Invagination
The terms atlantoaxial impaction, cranial settling, and basilar invagination are used to
describe the superior migration of the odontoid. Basilar invagination may result in brain
stem compression, including injury to the respiratory center. The anterior spinal artery
and vertebral arteries also may be compromised, leading to vertebrobasilar
insufficiency, transient ischemic attacks, or sudden death.6
Subaxial Instability
Inflammation and erosion of the zygapophyseal joints and surrounding bursae undermine
their stability, leading to laxity and subluxation of the subaxial spine.
C3-4 and C4-5 are the most commonly affected levels.
Lower cervical spine involvement is observed in more severe cases.
This instability pattern is a relatively late manifestation, and the reported frequency of subaxial
subluxation ranges from 7% to 29% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.7
Multilevel subluxation may lead to a staircase appearance on lateral radiographs and is
associated with kyphotic deformity.
Subaxial subluxation is best appreciated on flexion and extension radiographs.
Workup
Presentation may vary from asymptomatic patients to those with pain, deformity, and
neurologic deficits.
Neck pain and stiffness often are associated with occipital headaches because of irritation of
the greater occipital nerve, which is a branch of the C2 nerve root.

Patients may report paresthesia in the lateral aspect of the neck and clavicles and over the
shoulders, often attributable to subaxial cervical stenosis.
Patients with cervical spinal cord compression may demonstrate clinical signs of cervical
myelopathy.
Vertebrobasilar insufficiency may cause vertigo, nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, and dysarthria.
Laboratory analysis: Anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and increases in serum globulin
levels are seen in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid factor is a high-affinity autoantibody against immunoglobulin, has long served as
a diagnostic marker of rheumatoid arthritis, and is implicated in its pathogenesis.
In general, rheumatoid factor should be ordered only for patients with polyarticular joint
inflammation for more than 6 weeks.
Rheumatoid factor may be positive in healthy individuals.
A negative rheumatoid factor does not rule out the disease because rheumatoid arthritis may
be seronegative in 15% of patients.

Workup
The clinical presentation of rheumatoid arthritis is variable and ranges from
asymptomatic patients to those with pain, deformity, and neurologic deficits. The
cervical spine often is affected, and patients often complain of joint pain and stiffness,
most pronounced in the mornings and after periods of rest. Activity tends to improve
symptoms. As a result of atlantoaxial instability, patients may report a sensation of the
head falling forward, particularly during flexion of the neck. Myelopathic findings may
include a wide-based ataxic gait; diminished manual dexterity; muscle weakness; and, in
more severe patients, spasticity and urinary incontinence.
Physical examination may reveal tenderness with palpation over the axial skeleton and
limited range of motion of the neck. Loss of cervical lordosis also may be appreciated.
Diffuse peripheral joint involvement characterized by heat, swelling, tenderness, and
loss of motion may be present. Nodules secondary to local inflammation may be present
over the extensor surfaces of the hands and feet.

When rheumatoid arthritis is clinically suspected, laboratory studies may be helpful in
confirming the diagnosis. A positive rheumatoid factor is present in approximately 85%
of patients; however, it is not specific for rheumatoid arthritis and may be present in
healthy individuals. Also, a negative rheumatoid factor does not rule out rheumatoid
arthritis; rather, the arthritis is termed seronegative. This is the case in approximately
15% of patients. During the first year of illness, rheumatoid factor is more likely to be
negative, with some individuals converting to seropositive status over time. In addition,
rheumatoid factor is observed in patients with other illnesses, such as Sjögren
syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, and chronic infections, and in approximately
10% of the healthy population. Because of this low specificity, new serologic tests have
been developed that test for the presence of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies or anti-
cyclic citrullinated protein. Similar to rheumatoid factor, these tests are positive in only a
proportion (67%) of all patients with rheumatoid arthritis but are rarely positive if
rheumatoid arthritis is not present, resulting in a specificity of approximately 95%.
Measurement of antibodies directed against cyclic citrullinated protein is associated with
a 95% specificity for rheumatoid arthritis.8 Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive
protein level, complete blood cell count with differential, a complete metabolic panel,
liver enzyme levels, and other immunologic tests (such as an antinuclear antibody test)
also are suggested to evaluate for other causes of inflammation.
Imaging Studies
Lateral radiographs are the most helpful for initial evaluation of the cervical spine.
Flexion-extension lateral cervical radiographs are useful for evaluation of dynamic instability.
Most patients have atlantoaxial instability; therefore, the posterior and anterior atlanto-dens
intervals (ADIs) should be measured on lateral radiographs9 (Figure 2).

Although an anterior ADI greater than 5 mm is considered diagnostic of atlantoaxial
subluxation, it has been shown that measurement of the posterior ADI is a more reliable
predictor of neurologic deficit. An anterior ADI greater than 10 mm or a posterior ADI
less than 14 mm is associated with an increased risk of injury to the spinal cord and are
indications for surgical stabilization. MRI is indicated if myelopathy is present or if plain
radiographs demonstrate atlantoaxial subluxation with a posterior ADI less than 14 mm,
any basilar invagination, or subaxial stenosis with a canal diameter less than 14 mm.
The diagnosis of superior migration of the odontoid may be difficult because of bony
erosion of the odontoid and difficulty in defining the margins of the foramen magnum
on plain radiographs. Additional evaluation via CT or MRI is recommended. The
cervicomedullary angle can be measured by drawing a line along the anterior aspect of
the cervical spinal cord and the medulla. This angle normally is between 135° and 175°.
With progressive craniocervical disease, the brain stem angulates ventrally over the
displaced odontoid process, leading to a more acute cervicomedullary angle2 (Figure 4).

Medical Management
Immunosuppressive, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are administered to
reduce the rate of bone and cartilage damage.

9/3/26, 4:29 PM

12/40

Anti-inflammatories and analgesic agents improve pain and stiffness but do not prevent joint
damage or slow disease progression.
Two main types of DMARDs: traditional and biologics
Traditional DMARDs include methotrexate (MTX), leflunomide, azathioprine,
hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine. Traditional DMARDs act via various mechanisms to
interfere with the inflammatory cascade.
Biologic DMARDs inhibit TNF-α and interleukin-1 and usually are prescribed after evidence of
disease progression is observed despite management with corticosteroids and traditional
therapy.
TNF-α is a macrophage-derived cytokine that mediates inflammation and subsequent joint
destruction.
Prudent perioperative management of DMARDs is required to optimize surgical outcome.
Coordination with a rheumatologist is recommended. A balance must be struck between
minimizing potential surgical complications and maintaining disease control for postoperative
rehabilitation.
Some DMARDs, particularly TNF-α inhibitors, are stopped one drug half-life before surgery to
reduce infection (etanercept, adalimumab, and infliximab are stopped 1 week, 4 weeks, and 4
weeks preoperatively, respectively) and are started again after healing has occurred
(approximately 2 weeks postoperatively; Figure 5; Resource 1).
Figure 5 Algorithm shows perioperative management of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α
inhibitors. (Reproduced with permission from Saleh KJ, Kurdi AJ, El-Othmani MM, et al:

Glucocorticoids are a common treatment option because of their low cost and fast-acting
nature.
Prolonged use of corticosteroids decreases bone quality, impairs wound healing, and
compromises the immune system.
NSAIDs were the first-line treatment option for pain and stiffness in patients with rheumatoid
arthritis; however, their use currently is more limited to adjunctive therapy with DMARDS.
Aspirin is the most widely used NSAID, and it causes irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase,
thereby inhibiting platelet function and thrombosis.10
NSAIDs should be withheld up to 10 days preoperatively to prevent an increased risk of
perioperative bleeding. Platelets have a life span of 8 to 10 days and an estimated turnover
rate of 10% per day if aspirin is discontinued, resulting in normal platelet cyclooxygenase-1
activity in approximately 10 days.

Medical Management
DMARDS have substantially improved patient survival and decreased the number of
patients who require orthopaedic management.11 The most commonly used DMARD for
first-line management of rheumatoid arthritis is MTX, which is a cytotoxic drug
prescribed to reduce the progression of joint destruction. MTX inhibits dihydrofolate
reductase and other enzymes that inhibit cytokine production. MTX has been shown to
inhibit the expression of receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ B ligand, which prevents
osteoclast formation.12 Leflunomide inhibits pyrimidine synthesis13 and increases the
risk of surgical wound infection. Leflunomide should be discontinued 1 to 2 weeks
preoperatively and reinstated 1 to 2 weeks postoperatively.
Some biologic agents include abatacept, etanercept, infliximab, rituximab, and
tocilizumab. Their design is highly specific and targeted to affect immune function. The
overarching function of biologics includes interfering with cytokine function or
production, inhibiting the second signal required for T-cell activation, and depleting B
cells or inhibiting factors that activate B cells (rituximab and belimumab). Because of the
role that TNF-α plays in the immune response through the apoptosis of infected cells and

the destruction of intracellular organisms, patients being treated with TNF-α inhibitors
have an increased risk for opportunistic infections.14,15
In most patients with rheumatoid arthritis, treatment will include monotherapy or a
combination of therapies. Before starting, resuming, or substantially increasing the
dosage of biologics or nonbiologics, patients are screened for hepatitis B and C,
especially if they have a history of intravenous drug abuse or if they engage in high-risk
sexual behaviors. In other patients, a purified protein derivative skin test or an
interferon-γ release assay is conducted to establish a baseline for latent tuberculosis
infection. A baseline chest radiograph also should be obtained because some of these
medications may cause interstitial lung disease.
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis who undergo elective orthopaedic surgery do not
have an increased short-term risk for infection if MTX is continued throughout the
procedure.16,17 Inflammatory flare-ups have been observed if MTX has been
discontinued perioperatively.18 For patients with disease that is well controlled via MTX,
treatment should not be discontinued preoperatively.
For patients receiving long-term corticosteroid therapy, administration of a physiologic
dose of glucocorticoids at the time of surgery followed by a gradual tapering to
preoperative doses is beneficial in reducing the risk of acute perioperative adrenal
insufficiency.19
Considerations for Surgical Management
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis typically present with more comorbidities and risk factors
than the general population.
Inflammation related to rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, such as
ankylosing spondylitis, has been presumed to contribute to lower bone mineral densities and
increased risk of vertebral fractures.20,21
Radiographs should be obtained before elective surgery requiring intubation to assess for
cervical instability.

Considerations for Surgical Management
Chronic systemic inflammation causes an increased risk of cardiovascular problems,
such as venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, and
stroke. Mortality associated with cardiovascular disease in patients with rheumatoid
arthritis is approximately 50% higher than the risk in the general population.22 An
increased risk also exists for rheumatoid arthritis–associated deaths secondary to
interstitial lung disease.
In a study of 113 patients with rheumatoid arthritis who underwent total hip or knee
arthroplasty, 69 of the patients (61%) had cervical spine instability.23,24 Because
intubation often requires hyperextension of the neck, it also is important to clinically
assess cervical range of motion preoperatively.
Patients undergoing spine fusion have an increased risk for infection and revision
surgery.25 Patients with rheumatoid arthritis have a higher risk of implant-related
complications.26
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis have an increased risk for adjacent segment disease
after lumbar spinal fusion.27 Although adult patients with spinal deformity and
rheumatoid arthritis have an increased risk for medical complications, morbidity and
long-term outcomes are similar to those of patients without rheumatoid arthritis.28
Surgical Indications and Management
The primary goal of surgical management is to prevent or arrest the progression of permanent
neurologic injury.
Indications for surgical management include
Considerable atlantoaxial instability (>10 mm of motion between flexion and extension)
(Figure 6)
Posterior ADI less than 14 mm
Cervicomedullary angle less than 135°2

finding that may predict complete neural recovery after decompressive surgery)29

myelopathy demonstrate reducible atlantoaxial subluxation. A, Flexion radiograph shows an

C1-C2 Posterior Cervical Fusion
Before the adoption of modern surgical instrumentation, the traditional method of C1-C2
fusion involved the use of sublaminar wires.
C1-C2 transarticular screws, described by Magerl and Seeman in the 1980s, was a major
advance in posterior C1-C2 fixation (Figure 7).
Transarticular screws were associated with improved mechanical integrity and higher fusion
rates.
Careful preoperative planning is required for CT reconstruction to confirm that adequate bone
exists to allow for passage of the screws without injury to the vertebral arteries. CT
angiography may be considered to better assess the vertebral artery.

The use of transarticular screws may not be feasible in patients with a large or aberrant
foramen transversarium in C2 (Figure 8).
C1 lateral mass and C2 pars/pedicle instrumentation currently is the most commonly used
technique.
Goel and Laheri30 first described use of C1 lateral mass screws, which was then popularized by
Harms and Melcher31 in 2001. Screws are inserted into the lateral mass of C1 and into the pars
or the pedicle of C2 and are then secured by rods bilaterally (Figure 9).
This construct is associated with lower risk to the vertebral arteries, and the trajectories for
placement are easier to obtain compared with transarticular instrumentation.
Alternative techniques include the use of C1 lateral mass screws in combination with C2
laminar screws (Figure 10). This is a useful technique if solid fusion is desired but preoperative
CT scans show that C1-C2 transarticular screws and C1-C2 screws are not feasible and
potentially dangerous. Preoperative CT is advised to ensure an adequate corridor for a screw
in the C2 laminae.
In patients with atlantoaxial subluxation with basilar invagination, an occiput to C2 fusion with
possible decompression with a C1 laminectomy is indicated.

C1-C2 Posterior Cervical Fusion
Early wiring constructs for C1-C2 posterior cervical fusion often were supplemented by
halo immobilization to impart additional stability. Transarticular screw fixation later
provided substantially greater mechanical stability. With transarticular screw placement,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Inflammatory Spinal Arthritides
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000057
21/40

the vertebral artery is the structure most at risk, particularly with caudal trajectory of the
instrumentation and especially in patients with a large or aberrant vertebral artery.
Misplacement of a transarticular screw caudally is more common than misplacement
cranially given the difficulty in achieving the necessary angle of approach, particularly in
patients with thoracic kyphosis32 (Figure 11). Relatively, injury to the spinal cord is much
less likely given the large size of the spinal canal in the upper cervical spine and the
trajectory of the instrumentation. The occiput-C1 joint may be injured if the screw
trajectory is directed too cranially.
Surgeons must recognize the structures at risk during C1 lateral mass fixation. Ventral to
the C1 arch lies the internal carotid artery and the hypoglossal nerve; therefore,
unicortical C1 lateral mass screws often are used.
Often, a fashioned interspinous iliac crest autograft or a structural bone allograft is
placed between the posterior arch of C1 and the posterior spinous process and superior
laminar surface of C2 to facilitate fusion. The rate of C1-C2 pseudarthrosis is decreased
by extension of the fusion to the occiput; however, this substantially limits rotational
range of motion. If solid fusion is obtained, the periodontoid pannus tends to regress
and slow the progression of cranial settling. Transoral odontoid resection rarely is
indicated and may be considered in patients with residual anterior cord compression
because of pannus formation that fails to resorb with time after posterior spinal fusion.

Ankylosing Spondylitis
Epidemiology and Natural History
Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder characterized by progressive
involvement of the sacroiliac joints and the axial spine.
Ankylosing spondylitis is seronegative, which means rheumatoid factor is absent in the serum.
Ankylosing spondylitis occurs in approximately 0.2% to 0.3% of the US population, usually
beginning in patients in their twenties, with a male-to-female ratio of 3:1.
There is a genetic predisposition; however, the mode of inheritance remains unknown.
Most patients with ankylosing spondylitis are positive for HLA-B27, a class I surface antigen
encoded by the B locus in the major histocompatibility complex.
Most individuals positive for HLA-B27 do not have inflammatory arthropathy of the spine.

The presence of enthesitis, or inflammation at a site of attachment of tendon, ligament,
or muscle to bone (enthesis), is a distinguishing characteristic of the
spondyloarthropathies from other forms of arthritis. This contrasts against rheumatoid
arthritis, which primarily affects the synovial lining. Inflammation of the entheses leads
to bony erosions followed by new or reactive bone formation and eventual ankylosis.
Inflammation of the anulus fibrosus in patients with ankylosing spondylitis leads to the
formation of bridging syndesmophytes. Synovitis, such as that in the sacroiliac joint, may
be a secondary event after initiation with an enthesitis.33
HLA-B27 is present in more than 90% of Caucasian patients with ankylosing spondylitis
and is associated with a prevalence of 7% to 8% in a similar population without
ankylosing spondylitis.34
Genetic factors predispose patients to seronegative spondyloarthropathies, and
environmental factors play a role as triggers of the inflammatory response in genetically
predisposed individuals. A few theories exist regarding the link between HLA-B27 and
ankylosing spondylitis. One theory includes the binding of HLA-B27 to a peptide in the
joint, which stimulates a degenerative cascade. Another is that HLA-B27 may play a role
in alteration of the microbiome, which may contribute to the pathogenesis of
spondyloarthritis.35 A T-cell autoimmune response against HLA-B27 also may play a role
in the disease.
Clinical History and Physical Examination
Patients present in early adulthood with chronic low back and gluteal pain and stiffness.
Morning back stiffness that lasts for 30 minutes or more, diminishes with activity, and returns
after inactivity is characteristic of inflammatory back pain.
Inflammatory back pain occurs in 70% to 80% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis.36,37
Patients have decreased chest expansion (<2 cm) relative to other individuals secondary to
costovertebral joint involvement.
Patients also may present with a kyphotic deformity in the spine, which is the result of multiple
microfractures that occur over time.

The nonspinal manifestations of ankylosing spondylitis include large peripheral joint (hip and
shoulder) arthritis, anterior uveitis and iritis, pulmonary fibrosis, renal amyloidosis, ascending
aortic abnormalities (stenosis, aortitis, and regurgitation), and cardiac conduction
abnormalities.
The diagnosis is established in patients who have had back pain for 3 or more consecutive
months before age 45 years, who have had plain radiographs or MRIs confirm sacroiliitis, and
who have had at least one clinical or laboratory finding characteristic of ankylosing
spondylitis.38,39
No single clinical feature, laboratory test, or imaging study is sufficient to establish the
diagnosis.
Referral to a rheumatologist should be considered in adolescents and young adults with
unexplained back pain for more than 3 months.

Clinical History and Physical Examination
Patients with ankylosing spondylitis often present in their twenties or thirties. Back pain
is greatest in the early morning after awakening and is increased by periods of inactivity.
Patients may awaken at night from pain, particularly during the second half of the night
after prolonged immobilization. Pain often is localized to the gluteal and sacroiliac
regions initially. Patients may complain of alternating buttock pain.
Patients may endorse sciatica-like symptoms, which usually are the result of sciatic nerve
irritation at the level of the piriformis muscle. As the disease advances, the back pain
becomes more persistent.
Palpation over the sacroiliac joints reveals pain in most patients. The FABER (flexion,
abduction, external rotation) maneuver may provoke pain in the sacroiliac joints. The
Gaenslen test (pressure on a hyperextended thigh with a contralateral flexed hip) also
may provoke sacroiliac joint pain.
HLA-B27 testing may be useful in young patients with early disease for whom the
differential diagnosis may be narrowed by the presence of HLA-B27. Inflammatory
markers, such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate, may be elevated. Both rheumatoid

Imaging Studies
The earliest radiographic sign of ankylosing spondylitis is erosion on the iliac side of the
sacroiliac joint.
Sacroiliitis is a bilateral and symmetric process in patients with ankylosing spondylitis. Initially,
areas of joint surface erosions may be present, with subsequent proliferation of bone possibly
leading to ankylosis.
A Ferguson pelvic tilt radiograph, with the x-ray beam directed 15° cephalad, improves
visualization of the anterior sacroiliac joint.
Sacroiliac joint fusion typically is followed by cephalad spinal progression.
AP and lateral views of the spine will show characteristic squaring of the vertebral bodies and
marginal syndesmophytes (Figures 12 and 13).

Thin, vertically oriented calcifications of the anulus fibrosus and anterior and posterior
longitudinal ligaments are termed syndesmophytes. A proliferation of marginal
syndesmophytes leads to the characteristic bamboo spine appearance (Figure 14). These
patients typically have diffuse ossification of the disk space without large osteophyte
formation.

help identify noncontiguous fractures.
MRI is helpful in patients with nonankylosed levels in which a diskoligamentous injury may
have occurred and in patients with neurologic deficits that necessitate investigation of the
spinal canal to assess for causes of neurologic injury, such as epidural hematoma.40

Imaging Studies
An AP supine view of the pelvis should be the first imaging study obtained in the
diagnosis of sacroiliitis. Other diagnostic imaging modalities include scintigraphy, CT, and
MRI. Scintigraphy is sensitive to inflammation in the sacroiliac joints but lacks specificity.
CT detects early bony changes but is unable to demonstrate active inflammation. MRI
can detect active inflammation, making it the best imaging modality for early detection
and also for young women in whom sacroiliitis is suspected to decrease radiographic
exposure.
In patients with ankylosing spondylitis, the zygapophyseal joints and costovertebral
joints also may be fused. As the disease progresses, a loss of lumbar lordosis and

The chin-brow vertical angle can be measured to determine the degree of deformity.
This is the angle between a line connecting the chin and brow and a vertical line. This
angle aids in determining the amount of correction necessary during an osteotomy.
Although all patients with hyperostotic conditions of the spine have a high risk for
neurologic injury after trauma, patients with ankylosing spondylitis have increased rates
of neurologic injury compared with patients with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
(DISH).
Another complication of ankylosing spondylitis is spondylodiscitis, a destructive lesion of
the disk and its surrounding vertebral bodies. MRI reveals increased activity in the
central portion of the vertebral end plate. The cause of these lesions may be localized
inflammation or minor trauma. Surgical fusion is considered for refractory cases.
Management
In general, ankylosing spondylitis is managed by rheumatologists; however, prolonged delay in
diagnosis usually is the result of failed recognition by other physicians.41
Treatment goals include reducing symptoms, improving and maintaining spinal flexibility, and
decreasing complications associated with the disease.
Exercise therapy and NSAIDs are first-line treatment option for the management of ankylosing
spondylitis.
For patients with symptoms not controlled by NSAID therapy or in whom NSAIDs are
associated with unacceptable adverse effects, the use of TNF-α inhibitors (ie, infliximab,
etanercept, adalimumab) are considered.

Physicians must be familiar with the clinical signs and symptoms of ankylosing
spondylitis to facilitate early diagnosis and management. Short symptom duration and a
positive C-reactive protein level at baseline currently are the best predictors for a good
response to TNF-α therapy.
Spine Trauma
Any patient with ankylosing spondylitis who presents with a sudden onset of back or neck pain
must undergo workup for a fracture.
These fractures are considered unstable because they extend across all three columns and
create two rigid segments with long lever arms.
Rapid neurologic deterioration may result from spinal instability or hematoma formation.
Most fractures are in the cervical spine, particularly between the mid-cervical to
cervicothoracic junction (Figure 3).
The risk of traumatic cervical spine injury is substantially higher in patients with ankylosing
spondylitis than in the healthy population.
Fractures typically are extension-type three-column fractures.
Most fractures may be managed with the use of posterior instrumentation alone.
Long instrumented constructs are advisable because of the long lever arms of the ankylosed
spine and the osteoporosis typically observed in these patients.
A high mortality rate, greater than 50%, may be noted in patients with ankylosing spondylitis
who are elderly, who have complete cord lesions, or in whom pulmonary complications occur
after fracture.
Spinal Deformity
Surgical management may be considered to correct substantial kyphosis and sagittal
malalignment.
The goals of deformity surgery are restoration of sagittal balance and horizontal gaze.
Pedicle subtraction osteotomies can achieve as much as 30° of sagittal correction.
Cervicothoracic pedicle subtraction osteotomy may be performed in patients with a fixed
flexion deformity. In the most severe patients, a chin-on-chest deformity is present, making it
difficult to maintain a forward gaze and perform personal hygiene tasks.

Spinal Deformity
A minimal amount of trauma may result in a devastating fracture in a patient with an
ankylosed spine because it is much more brittle.
Intraoperatively, more bleeding tends to occur. Often, intraoperative navigation is
helpful to facilitate instrumentation because bony landmarks are not distinguishable as
a result of diffuse ossification. Instrumentation is recommended for at least three
segments above and below the fracture because of the long lever arm of the fracture.
In patients with trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, and cervicothoracic kyphosis, the neck
should be maintained in the premorbid flexed position until definitive management can
be performed. Extension of the neck may lead to displacement of a previously aligned
fracture and subsequent neurologic injury.
Cervicothoracic pedicle subtraction osteotomy is performed at C7-T1 and is associated
with the advantages of being caudal to the entry of the vertebral artery in the transverse
foramen and a larger canal diameter. In measuring global sagittal alignment, care should
be taken to evaluate the contribution of hip flexion contractures to sagittal
malalignment.

patients with psoriasis.
HLA-B27 is positive in approximately 50% of patients and usually is more common in patients
in whom spondyloarthropathy occurs.

Psoriatic Spondylitis
Factors that contribute to the diagnosis of psoriatic spondylitis are a medical or family
history of psoriasis, negative rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody test results,
and radiographic images demonstrating joint destruction. Spinal involvement does not
occur in an ascending manner, such as in ankylosing spondylitis, but may appear
randomly. Joint ankylosis occurs less commonly than in ankylosing spondylitis. Dissimilar
from ankylosing spondylitis, diskovertebral erosions and axial ankylosis occur in a
noncontiguous asymmetric pattern, with marginal and nonmarginal syndesmophytes.
Patients with psoriatic spondylitis also may have a synovial proliferative process in the
cervical spine similar to that in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Reactive Arthritis
Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune response to infection that may result in postinfectious
arthritis, with aseptic inflammation in joints and other organs.
Manifestations include inflammatory arthritis of large joints, inflammation of the eyes in the
form of conjunctivitis or uveitis, and urethritis in men or cervicitis in women.
It is the most common type of inflammatory polyarthritis in young men and primarily affects
the lower extremity joints and the low back.
The disease is the result of an environmental factor, usually a specific infection, such as with a
genitourinary or gastrointestinal pathogen, and a genetically susceptible host.
HLA-B27 positivity increases the risk of reactive arthritis.

Reactive Arthritis
Often, the inciting infection is cured before the time of presentation (up to 6 weeks
before) in patients with reactive arthritis, which makes determination of the initial cause
a challenge. The triad of urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis is observed in less than
one-third of patients. The main goal of management is to identify and eradicate the
underlying infectious source, if still present, and provide supportive care.
Dissimilar from ankylosing spondylitis, asymmetric sacroiliitis is more commonly
observed in patients with spinal involvement. Spondylitis is discontinuous in its
involvement of the axial skeleton and is characterized by nonmarginal syndesmophytes.
Enteropathic Arthritis
Spondylitis can occur in combination with ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease.
Clinical presentation and management are identical to that for ankylosing spondylitis.
80% of patients who have spinal involvement are HLA-B27 positive.
Spondylitis occurs in 3% to 4% of patients with Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, and
radiographic sacroiliitis occurs in 10%.
TNF-α inhibitors are effective agents for bowel and articular disease.42

Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis
DISH is an enthesopathy of unknown etiology characterized by flowing anterior ossifications of
the spine and ossification of peripheral tendinous insertions.
It often is asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.
Clinical symptoms include neck and back pain and stiffness, which often is worse in the
morning.44
It typically occurs in patients older than 50 years, with a prevalence that increases with age.
The diagnostic radiographic criteria for DISH include flowing anterior ossification of at least
four contiguous vertebral bodies, relative intervertebral disk preservation, and the absence of
inflammatory changes and ankylosis of the sacroiliac joint.45
Dissimilar from patients with ankylosing spondylitis who have marginal syndesmophytes,
patients with DISH have osteophytes beyond the corners of the vertebral bodies, and these
syndesmophytes are referred to as nonmarginal.
DISH usually does not involve the sacroiliac joints.
DISH is more common in patients with diabetes mellitus or gout.
If a spinal fracture is present, ankylosis of the spine increases the proximal and distal lever
arms, which may result in unstable fracture patterns.
Patients with a history of trauma and neck or back pain who have DISH should be evaluated
for occult fracture via CT.

Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis
In contrast to patients with ankylosing spondylitis, patients with DISH have large,
nonmarginal syndesmophytes. Nonmarginal syndesmophytes give a flowing candle wax
appearance. In addition, DISH typically affects older patients and spares the sacroiliac
joints. It most commonly presents in the thoracic spine, followed by the cervical and
lumbar spine. Thoracic and lumbar involvement lead to stiffness and pain, whereas
cervical involvement results in large anterior osteophytes that can cause dysphagia and
